title: Chapter 20. Of Dominion Paternal and Despotic
paragraphs: A commonwealth by acquisition is one in which the sovereign power is acquired by force. It is acquired by force when men, either singly or many together by plurality of votes, for fear of death or bondage, authorise all the actions of the man, or assembly, who holds their lives and liberty in his power.

This kind of dominion, or sovereignty, differs from sovereignty by institution only in this: that men who choose their sovereign do it from fear of one another, and not from fear of him whom they institute; whereas in this case they subject themselves to the man they are afraid of. In both cases they act from fear — which should be noted by those who hold that all such covenants as proceed from fear of death or violence are void. If that were so, no man in any kind of commonwealth could be obliged to obedience. It is true that in a commonwealth once instituted or acquired, promises proceeding from fear of death or violence are no covenants, and do not oblige, when the thing promised is contrary to the laws. But the reason is not that the promise was made under fear; it is that the person promising had no right in the thing promised. Also, when a man may lawfully perform a promise and does not, what releases him is not the invalidity of the covenant, but the sentence of the sovereign. Otherwise, whenever a man lawfully promised, he would unlawfully break — but when the sovereign, who is the actor, acquits him, then he is acquitted by the one who extorted the promise, as by the author of such release.

But the rights and consequences of sovereignty are the same in both. The sovereign's power cannot, without his consent, be transferred to another; he cannot forfeit it; he cannot be accused by any of his subjects of injury; he cannot be punished by them; he is the judge of what is necessary for peace, and judge of doctrines; he is sole legislator, and supreme judge of controversies, and of the times and occasions of war and peace. To him belongs the choice of magistrates, counsellors, commanders, and all other officers and ministers, and the determination of rewards and punishments, of honour and order. The reasons for all this are the same as those given in the previous chapter for the same rights and consequences of sovereignty by institution.

Dominion is acquired in two ways: by generation, and by conquest. The right of dominion by generation is the right a parent has over his children, and is called PATERNAL. And it is not derived from generation in such a way that the parent has dominion over his child merely because he begot him; it comes from the child's consent, either expressed or declared by other sufficient signs. As to generation, God has ordained for man a helper, and there are always two who are equally parents. Dominion over the child therefore should belong equally to both, and the child be equally subject to both — which is impossible, for no man can obey two masters. And whereas some have attributed the dominion to the man only, as being of the more excellent sex, they miscalculate. There is not always such a difference of strength or prudence between man and woman that the right can be settled without war. In commonwealths this controversy is decided by the civil law, and for the most part (though not always) the sentence is in favour of the father, because for the most part commonwealths have been founded by the fathers, not by the mothers, of families. But the question now lies in the state of mere nature, where there are supposed no laws of matrimony, no laws for the education of children — only the law of nature, and the natural inclination of the sexes to each other and to their children. In this condition of mere nature, either the parents between themselves dispose of the dominion over the child by contract, or they do not. If they do, the right passes according to the contract. We find in history that the Amazons contracted with the men of the neighbouring countries, to whom they resorted for offspring, that the male issue should be sent back to the fathers but the female should remain with them; so the dominion of the females was in the mother.

If there is no contract, the dominion is in the mother. For in the condition of mere nature, where there are no matrimonial laws, it cannot be known who the father is unless the mother declares it; and so the right of dominion over the child depends on her will, and is consequently hers. Further: the infant is first in the mother's power — she may nourish it or expose it. If she nourishes it, it owes its life to her, and is therefore obliged to obey her rather than any other; and so dominion over it is hers. But if she exposes it and another finds and nourishes it, the dominion is in the one who nourishes it. The child should obey the one who preserves it, because the preservation of life being the end for which one man becomes subject to another, every man is presumed to promise obedience to the one in whose power it lies to save or destroy him.

If the mother is the father's subject, the child is in the father's power; and if the father is the mother's subject (as when a sovereign queen marries one of her subjects), the child is subject to the mother, because the father too is her subject.

If a man and a woman, monarchs of two distinct kingdoms, have a child, and contract concerning who shall have the dominion over him, the right of dominion passes by the contract. If they make no contract, the dominion follows the dominion of the place of his residence: for the sovereign of each country has dominion over all who reside in it.

He who has dominion over the child has dominion also over the children's children. For he who has dominion over the person of a man has dominion over all that is his — without which, dominion would be only a title, without effect.
The right of succession to paternal dominion runs the same way as the right of succession to monarchy, of which I have already said enough in the previous chapter.

Dominion acquired by conquest, or by victory in war, is what some writers call DESPOTICAL, from despotes, which means a lord or master; it is the dominion of master over servant. This dominion is acquired by the victor when the vanquished, to avoid the present stroke of death, covenants either in express words or by other sufficient signs of the will that, so long as his life and the liberty of his body are allowed him, the victor shall have the use of them at his pleasure. And after such a covenant is made, the vanquished is a SERVANT — and not before. For by the word 'servant' (whether derived from servire, to serve, or from servare, to save — which I leave to grammarians to dispute) is not meant a captive kept in prison or in bonds until the master who took him, or who bought him from one who did, shall decide what to do with him. Such men, commonly called slaves, are under no obligation at all, and may justly break their bonds or the prison, and kill or carry away captive their master. 'Servant' here means rather one who, being taken, has been allowed bodily liberty, and on his promise neither to run away nor to do violence to his master, is trusted by him.

It is not therefore the victory that gives the right of dominion over the vanquished, but the vanquished man's own covenant. Nor is he obliged because he is conquered — that is, beaten and taken, or put to flight — but because he comes in and submits to the victor. Nor is the victor obliged, by an enemy's surrendering (without any promise of life), to spare him for that surrender to discretion: it obliges the victor no longer than as, in his own discretion, he shall think fit.

What men do when they ask (as it is now called) for quarter — what the Greeks called zogria, taking alive — is to evade the immediate fury of the victor by submission, and to compound for their life with ransom or service. And so the man who has quarter has not had his life given but deferred until further consideration. It is not a surrender on condition of life, but a surrender to discretion. His life is only then secure, and his service only then due, when the victor has trusted him with bodily liberty. For slaves who work in prisons or in fetters do not do so out of duty, but to avoid the cruelty of their taskmasters.

The master of the servant is also master of all the servant has, and may exact the use of it — that is, of his goods, his labour, his servants, and his children — as often as he thinks fit. For the servant holds his life from his master by the covenant of obedience: that is, by owning and authorising whatever the master shall do. And if the master, when the servant refuses, kills him, or casts him into bonds, or otherwise punishes him for his disobedience, the servant is himself the author of it, and cannot accuse him of injury.

In short, the rights and consequences of both paternal and despotical dominion are exactly the same as those of a sovereign by institution, and for the same reasons, which are set down in the previous chapter. So for a man who is monarch of several nations — having in one the sovereignty by institution of the people assembled, and in another by conquest, that is by the submission of each individual to avoid death or bondage — to demand more from the one nation than from the other on grounds of conquest, as being a conquered nation, is an act of ignorance of the rights of sovereignty. For the sovereign is absolute over both alike, or else there is no sovereignty at all; and so every man may lawfully protect himself, if he can, with his own sword — which is the condition of war.

By this it appears that a great family, if it is not part of some commonwealth, is in itself, as to the rights of sovereignty, a little monarchy — whether that family consists of a man and his children, of a man and his servants, or of a man with his children and servants together; in which the father, or master, is the sovereign. Yet a family is not properly a commonwealth, unless it is of such power, by its own numbers or by other opportunities, that it cannot be subdued without the hazard of war. For where a body of men is plainly too weak to defend themselves united, every one may use his own reason in time of danger to save his own life, either by flight or by submission to the enemy, as he shall think best — just as a very small company of soldiers surprised by an army may throw down their arms and ask for quarter, or run away, rather than be put to the sword. And so much shall suffice for what I find by speculation and deduction concerning sovereign rights, drawn from the nature, needs, and designs of men in erecting commonwealths and putting themselves under monarchs or assemblies entrusted with power enough for their protection.

Let us now consider what Scripture teaches on the same point. To Moses, the children of Israel say: 'Speak thou to us, and we will hear thee; but let not God speak to us, lest we die' (Exodus 20:19). This is absolute obedience to Moses. Concerning the right of kings, God himself, by the mouth of Samuel, says (1 Samuel 8:11–12 etc.): 'This shall be the right of the king you will have to reign over you. He shall take your sons, and set them to drive his chariots, and to be his horsemen, and to run before his chariots; and gather in his harvest; and to make his engines of war, and instruments of his chariots; and shall take your daughters to make perfumes, to be his cooks and bakers. He shall take your fields, your vineyards, and your olive yards, and give them to his servants. He shall take the tithe of your corn and wine, and give it to the men of his chamber, and to his other servants. He shall take your manservants, and your maidservants, and the choice of your youth, and employ them in his business. He shall take the tithe of your flocks; and you shall be his servants.' This is absolute power, summed up in the last words: 'you shall be his servants.' Again, when the people heard what power their king was to have, they still consented, saying (verse 19 etc.): 'We will be as all other nations, and our king shall judge our causes, and go before us, to conduct our wars.' Here is confirmed the right that sovereigns have, both to the militia and to all judicature — which contains as absolute a power as one man can possibly transfer to another. Again, King Solomon's prayer to God was this (1 Kings 3:9): 'Give to thy servant understanding, to judge thy people, and to discern between good and evil.' It belongs therefore to the sovereign to be judge, and to prescribe the rules of discerning good and evil; and these rules are laws; and so in him is the legislative power. Saul sought David's life; yet when it was in David's power to slay Saul, and his servants would have done it, David forbade them, saying (1 Samuel 24:9): 'God forbid I should do such an act against my lord, the anointed of God.' For the obedience of servants, St Paul says (Colossians 3:20): 'Servants, obey your masters in all things,' and (verse 22): 'Children, obey your parents in all things.' That is plain obedience in those who are subject to paternal or despotical dominion. Again (Matthew 23:2–3): 'The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses' chair, and therefore all that they shall bid you observe, that observe and do.' There again is plain obedience. And St Paul (Titus 3:2): 'Warn them that they subject themselves to princes, and to those that are in authority, and obey them.' This obedience is also plain. Lastly, our Saviour himself acknowledges that men ought to pay such taxes as kings impose, when he says, 'Give to Caesar what is Caesar's' — and paid such taxes himself. And that the king's word is enough to take anything from any subject when there is need, and that the king is judge of that need: for he himself, as king of the Jews, ordered his disciples to take the ass and the ass's colt to carry him into Jerusalem, saying (Matthew 21:2–3): 'Go into the village over against you, and you shall find an ass tied, and her colt with her; loose them, and bring them to me. And if any man asks you what you mean by it, say, The Lord has need of them; and they will let them go.' They are not to ask whether his necessity is a sufficient title, nor whether he is the judge of that necessity, but to acquiesce in the will of the Lord.

To these passages may also be added the one in Genesis (3:5): 'You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil'; and verse 11: 'Who told thee that thou wast naked? hast thou eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee thou shouldest not eat?' The faculty of judging good and evil, being forbidden under the name of the fruit of the tree of knowledge as a test of Adam's obedience, was the very thing the devil, to inflame the ambition of the woman (to whom that fruit already seemed beautiful), promised they would obtain by tasting it: that they should be as gods, knowing good and evil. Having both eaten, they did indeed take upon themselves God's office, which is the judicature of good and evil; but they acquired no new ability to distinguish rightly between them. And as for the saying that, having eaten, they saw they were naked, no one has interpreted that passage as if they had previously been blind and unable to see their own skins. The meaning is plain: it was then that they first judged their nakedness (in which it was God's will to create them) to be unseemly; and by being ashamed, they tacitly censured God himself. And thereupon God says, 'Hast thou eaten? etc.' — as if to say, 'Do you, who owe me obedience, take it upon yourself to judge of my commandments?' By which it is clearly, though allegorically, signified that the commands of those who have the right to command are not to be censured, or disputed, by their subjects.

So it plainly appears, to my understanding, both from reason and from Scripture, that the sovereign power — whether placed in one man, as in monarchy, or in one assembly of men, as in popular and aristocratic commonwealths — is as great as men can possibly imagine making it. And though men may fancy many evil consequences from so unlimited a power, the consequences of the lack of it — which is perpetual war of every man against his neighbour — are much worse. The condition of man in this life shall never be without inconveniences; but no great inconvenience happens in any commonwealth that does not proceed from the subjects' disobedience and breach of those covenants from which the commonwealth had its being. And whoever, thinking sovereign power too great, will seek to make it less, must subject himself to the power that can limit it — that is, to a greater.

The greatest objection is from practice, when men ask where, and when, such power has been acknowledged by subjects. But one may ask them in turn: when, or where, has there been a kingdom long free from sedition and civil war? In those nations whose commonwealths have been long-lived and have been destroyed only by foreign war, the subjects never disputed the sovereign power. In any case, an argument from the practice of men who have not sifted the matter to the bottom, and who have not by exact reasoning weighed the causes and nature of commonwealths, and who suffer daily the miseries that come from ignorance of these things, is invalid. For though in every part of the world men should lay the foundations of their houses on the sand, it could not be inferred from that that this is how it should be done. The skill of building and maintaining commonwealths consists in certain rules, as does arithmetic and geometry; not (as a game of tennis does) on practice alone. These rules neither poor men have had the leisure, nor men who have had the leisure have hitherto had the curiosity, or the method, to find out.

title: Chapter 21. Of the Liberty of Subjects
paragraphs: Liberty, or FREEDOM, properly signifies the absence of opposition — by which I mean external impediments to motion — and may be applied no less to irrational and inanimate things than to rational ones. For whatever is so tied, or hemmed in, that it cannot move except within a certain space, that space being determined by the opposition of some external body, we say it has no liberty to go further. So of all living creatures, while they are imprisoned or restrained with walls or chains; and of water, while it is held in by banks or vessels which otherwise would spread it into a larger space, we say they are not at liberty to move in the way they would without those external obstacles. But when the impediment to motion is in the constitution of the thing itself, we do not say it lacks liberty, but the power to move — as when a stone lies still, or a man is bound to his bed by sickness.

And according to this proper and generally received meaning of the word, a FREE-MAN is 'he who, in the things he is able by his strength and wit to do, is not hindered from doing what he has a will to do.' But when the words 'free' and 'liberty' are applied to anything but bodies, they are misused; for what is not subject to motion is not subject to impediment. So when it is said (for example) 'the way is free,' no liberty of the way is meant, but of those who walk in it without being stopped. When we say a gift is free, no liberty of the gift is meant but of the giver, who was not bound by any law or covenant to give it. So when we speak freely, it is not the liberty of voice or pronunciation, but of the man, whom no law has obliged to speak otherwise than he did. Finally, from the phrase 'free will' no liberty can be inferred to the will, desire, or inclination, but only to the man — which consists in this, that he finds no obstacle in doing what he has the will, the desire, or the inclination to do.

Fear and liberty are consistent. When a man throws his goods into the sea for fear that the ship may sink, he nevertheless does it very willingly, and may refuse to do it if he wishes; it is therefore the action of someone who was free. Likewise, a man sometimes pays his debt only for fear of imprisonment — and since no one was hindering him from keeping it back, it was the action of a man at liberty. In general, all actions which men do in commonwealths for fear of the law are actions the doers had the liberty to omit.

Liberty and necessity are consistent. As in water, which has not only the liberty but also the necessity of running down the channel, so also in the actions men voluntarily do: those actions, because they proceed from their will, proceed from liberty; and yet, because every act of a man's will, and every desire and inclination, proceeds from some cause — and those causes, in a continual chain (whose first link is in the hand of God, the first of all causes), proceed from necessity. So to one who could see the connection of those causes, the necessity of all men's voluntary actions would appear plain. And so God, who sees and disposes all things, sees also that man's liberty in doing what he wills is accompanied by the necessity of doing what God wills, and no more and no less. For though men may do many things which God does not command, and of which he is not therefore the author, they can have no passion or appetite for anything of which God's will is not the cause. And if his will did not secure the necessity of man's will, and consequently of everything that depends on man's will, the liberty of men would be a contradiction and an impediment to the omnipotence and the liberty of God. And so much (as far as the matter at hand) for that natural liberty, which alone is properly called liberty.

But as men, in order to attain peace and so to preserve themselves, have made an artificial man (which we call a commonwealth), so they have also made artificial chains, called civil laws, which they themselves, by mutual covenants, have fastened at one end to the lips of that man, or assembly, to whom they have given the sovereign power, and at the other end to their own ears. These bonds, weak in themselves, may nevertheless be made to hold by the danger, even where not by the difficulty, of breaking them.

It is only in relation to these bonds that I am now to speak of the liberty of subjects. Since there is no commonwealth in the world that can regulate every action and every word of men (that being impossible), it follows necessarily that in all kinds of action which the laws have passed over, men have the liberty of doing what their own reason shall suggest as most profitable to themselves. For if we take liberty in its proper sense — bodily liberty, that is, freedom from chains and prison — it would be very absurd for men to clamour, as they do, for a liberty they so plainly already enjoy. Again, if we take liberty as exemption from the laws, it is no less absurd for men to demand, as they do, a liberty by which all other men might be masters of their lives. And yet, absurd as it is, this is what they demand — not knowing that the laws have no power to protect them without a sword in the hands of a man, or men, to cause those laws to be executed. The liberty of a subject lies therefore only in those things which, in regulating their actions, the sovereign has passed over — such as the liberty to buy and sell, and otherwise to contract with one another, to choose their own dwelling, their own diet, their own trade of life, and to bring up their children as they themselves think fit, and the like.

Nevertheless, we are not to understand that by such liberty the sovereign power of life and death is either abolished or limited. For it has already been shown that nothing the sovereign representative does to a subject, on any pretext, can properly be called injustice or injury, because every subject is the author of every act the sovereign does — so that the sovereign never wants right to anything, except insofar as he himself is the subject of God, and is bound by that to observe the laws of nature. And so it may, and often does, happen in commonwealths that a subject may be put to death by the command of the sovereign power, and yet neither party do the other a wrong — as when Jephthah caused his daughter to be sacrificed. In that and similar cases, the one so dying had liberty to do the action for which he is nevertheless, without injury, put to death. The same holds when a sovereign prince puts to death an innocent subject. For though the action is against the law of nature, being contrary to equity (as was David's killing of Uriah), yet it was not an injury to Uriah; it was an injury to God. Not to Uriah, because the right to do as he pleased had been given to David by Uriah himself; and yet to God, because David was God's subject, and forbidden all iniquity by the law of nature. This distinction David himself, when he repented the act, plainly confirmed, saying, 'To thee only have I sinned.' In the same way the people of Athens, when they banished the most powerful man in their commonwealth for ten years, thought they committed no injustice — and yet they never inquired what crime he had done, but only what hurt he might do. They even commanded the banishment of men they did not know: every citizen brought his oyster-shell to the marketplace with the name written on it of the man he wanted banished, without actually accusing him; and they sometimes banished an Aristides for his reputation for justice, and sometimes a scurrilous jester such as Hyperbolus, to make a joke of it. And yet one cannot say that the sovereign people of Athens lacked the right to banish them, or that any Athenian lacked the liberty to jest or to be just.
The liberty that writers praise is the liberty of sovereigns, not of private men.

The liberty so frequently and so honourably mentioned in the histories and philosophy of the ancient Greeks and Romans, and in the writings and discourse of those who derive all their learning in politics from them, is not the liberty of particular men but the liberty of the commonwealth — which is the same as what every man would have if there were no civil laws and no commonwealth at all. And its effects are also the same. For as among masterless men there is perpetual war of every man against his neighbour — no inheritance to pass on to the son, or to expect from the father, no property of goods or lands, no security, but a full and absolute liberty in every particular man — so in states and commonwealths not dependent on one another, every commonwealth (not every man) has an absolute liberty to do whatever it shall judge (that is, whatever the man or assembly representing it shall judge) most conducive to its benefit. But with that they live in the condition of a perpetual war, on the verge of battle, with their frontiers armed and cannon planted against their neighbours all around. The Athenians and Romans were free — that is, free commonwealths; not that any particular men had the liberty to resist their own representative, but that their representative had the liberty to resist, or to invade, other peoples. The word LIBERTAS is written on the towers of the city of Lucca to this day in great letters; yet no one can infer from that that a private man has more liberty there, or more immunity from the service of the commonwealth, than he has in Constantinople. Whether a commonwealth is monarchical or popular, the freedom is still the same.

But it is easy for men to be deceived by the specious name of liberty, and for lack of judgement to distinguish between things, mistaking that for their private inheritance and birthright which is in fact only the right of the public. And when the same error is reinforced by the authority of men of high reputation for their writings on this subject, it is no wonder that it produces sedition and the overthrow of governments. In these western parts of the world, we are made to receive our opinions about the institution and the rights of commonwealths from Aristotle, Cicero, and other men, Greeks and Romans, who, living under popular states, derived those rights not from the principles of nature but transcribed them into their books out of the practice of their own commonwealths, which were popular — just as the grammarians describe the rules of language out of current practice, or the rules of poetry out of the poems of Homer and Virgil. And because the Athenians were taught (to keep them from wanting to change their government) that they were free men, and that all who lived under monarchy were slaves, Aristotle put it down in his Politics (book 6, chapter 2): 'In democracy, liberty is to be supposed: for it is commonly held that no man is free in any other government.' And as Aristotle, so Cicero and other writers have grounded their civil doctrine on the opinions of the Romans, who were taught to hate monarchy at first by those who, having deposed their sovereign, shared the sovereignty of Rome among themselves, and afterwards by their successors. By reading these Greek and Latin authors, men from childhood have gotten the habit, under a false show of liberty, of favouring tumults and of licentiously controlling the actions of their sovereigns — and then of controlling those controllers, at the cost of so much bloodshed that I think I may truly say that nothing has ever been so dearly bought as these western parts have bought the learning of the Greek and Latin tongues.

To come now to the particulars of the true liberty of a subject — that is, what are the things which, though commanded by the sovereign, a subject may nevertheless without injustice refuse to do — we must consider what rights we give away when we make a commonwealth; or (what is the same thing) what liberty we deny ourselves by owning all the actions, without exception, of the man or assembly we make our sovereign. For in the act of our submission lie both our obligation and our liberty; which must therefore be inferred by arguments taken from that act, since there is no obligation on any man which does not arise from some act of his own — for all men by nature are equally free. And because such arguments must be drawn either from the express words 'I authorise all his actions,' or from the intention of the man who submits himself to the sovereign's power (which intention is to be understood from the end for which he submits), the obligation and liberty of the subject are to be derived either from those words (or others equivalent) or else from the end of the institution of sovereignty — namely, the peace of the subjects among themselves and their defence against a common enemy.
Subjects have liberty to defend their own bodies, even against those who lawfully assault them.

First, then, since sovereignty by institution is by covenant of every one to every one, and sovereignty by acquisition is by covenants of the vanquished to the victor, or of child to parent, it is plain that every subject has liberty in all those things the right to which cannot by covenant be transferred. I have shown before, in chapter 14, that covenants not to defend one's own body are void. Therefore —

If the sovereign commands a man (even one justly condemned) to kill, wound, or maim himself, or not to resist those who assault him, or to abstain from the use of food, air, medicine, or any other thing without which he cannot live, that man still has the liberty to disobey.

If a man is interrogated by the sovereign, or by his authority, about a crime he himself has committed, he is not bound (without assurance of pardon) to confess it; because no man (as I have shown in the same chapter) can by covenant be obliged to accuse himself.

Again, the consent of a subject to sovereign power is contained in these words: 'I authorise, or take upon myself, all his actions.' In these there is no restriction at all of his own former natural liberty. For by allowing the sovereign to kill me, I am not bound to kill myself when he commands. It is one thing to say, 'Kill me, or my neighbour, if you please'; another thing to say, 'I will kill myself, or my neighbour.' It follows therefore that —

No man is bound by the words themselves to kill either himself or any other man; and consequently the obligation a man may sometimes have, on the command of the sovereign, to carry out any dangerous or dishonourable office depends not on the words of our submission, but on the intention — which is to be understood from the end of submission. When, therefore, our refusal to obey frustrates the end for which the sovereignty was ordained, there is no liberty to refuse; otherwise there is.

On this ground, a man who is commanded as a soldier to fight against the enemy, though his sovereign has right enough to punish his refusal with death, may nevertheless in many cases refuse, without injustice — as when he supplies an adequate soldier in his place; in that case he is not deserting the service of the commonwealth. And allowance is to be made for natural timorousness, not only in women (of whom no such dangerous duty is expected), but also in men of feminine courage. When armies fight, there is on one side or on both a running away; yet when they do it not from treachery but from fear, they are reckoned to do it not unjustly but dishonourably. For the same reason, to avoid battle is not injustice but cowardice. But the man who enrols himself as a soldier, or accepts a press-money, gives up the excuse of a timorous nature; and is obliged not only to go into the battle but also not to run from it without his captain's leave. And when the defence of the commonwealth requires at once the help of all who can bear arms, every man is obliged — for otherwise the institution of the commonwealth, which they have not the purpose or the courage to preserve, was in vain.

To resist the sword of the commonwealth in defence of another man, guilty or innocent, no man has liberty; because such liberty takes from the sovereign the means of protecting us, and is therefore destructive of the very essence of government. But if a great many men together have already unjustly resisted the sovereign power, or committed some capital crime for which every one of them expects death, have they not then the liberty to join together and assist and defend one another? Certainly they have; for they merely defend their lives, which the guilty man may do as well as the innocent. There was indeed injustice in the first breach of their duty; but their bearing of arms after the breach, though it be to maintain what they have done, is no new unjust act. And if it is only to defend their persons, it is not unjust at all. But the offer of pardon takes from those to whom it is offered the plea of self-defence, and makes their persistence in assisting or defending the rest unlawful.

As for other liberties, they depend on the silence of the law. Where the sovereign has prescribed no rule, the subject has liberty to do, or forbear, according to his own discretion. So such liberty is in some places greater and in some less; and at some times more, at other times less, according as those who hold the sovereignty shall think most convenient. For example, there was a time in England when a man might enter into his own land (and dispossess any who wrongfully held it) by force; but in later times that liberty of forcible entry was taken away by a statute made by the king in Parliament. And in some places of the world, men have the liberty of many wives; in others, no such liberty is allowed.

If a subject has a controversy with his sovereign — over a debt, or over the right of possession of lands or goods, or over any service required of him, or over any corporal or financial penalty grounded on a prior law — he has the same liberty to sue for his right as if it were against a fellow subject, and before such judges as are appointed by the sovereign. For since the sovereign demands by force of a prior law, and not by virtue of his power as such, he declares thereby that he requires no more than shall appear to be due by that law. The suit therefore is not contrary to the will of the sovereign; and consequently the subject has the liberty to demand the hearing of his cause, and a verdict according to that law. But if the sovereign demands or takes anything on the pretext of his power, no action of law lies in that case: for everything done by him in virtue of his power is done by the authority of every subject, and so anyone who brings an action against the sovereign brings it against himself.

If a monarch or sovereign assembly grants a liberty to all or any of his subjects, and while that grant stands he is disabled from providing for their safety, the grant is void — unless he directly renounces, or transfers, the sovereignty to another. For since he could openly (if it had been his will) have plainly renounced or transferred the sovereignty, and did not, it is to be understood that it was not his will; and that the grant proceeded from ignorance of the conflict between such a liberty and the sovereign power. So the sovereignty is still retained — and consequently all those powers which are necessary for exercising it, such as the power of war and peace, of judicature, of appointing officers and counsellors, of levying money, and the rest named in the eighteenth chapter.

The obligation of subjects to the sovereign is understood to last as long, and no longer, than the power lasts by which he is able to protect them. For the right men have by nature to protect themselves, when no one else can protect them, can by no covenant be relinquished. The sovereignty is the soul of the commonwealth; once it has departed from the body, the members no longer receive their motion from it. The end of obedience is protection; and wherever a man sees that protection — either in his own sword or in another's — nature applies his obedience to it, and his endeavour to maintain it. And though sovereignty, in the intention of those who make it, is immortal, in its own nature it is not only subject to violent death by foreign war, but also, through the ignorance and passions of men, carries in it, from its very institution, many seeds of a natural mortality, by internal discord.

If a subject is taken prisoner in war, or his person or his means of life are within the guards of the enemy, and his life and bodily liberty are given him on condition of becoming subject to the victor, he has the liberty to accept the condition; and having accepted it, he is the subject of the man who took him, because he had no other way to preserve himself. The case is the same if he is detained on the same terms in a foreign country. But if a man is held in prison or in bonds, or is not trusted with the liberty of his body, he cannot be understood to be bound by covenant to subjection, and may therefore, if he can, make his escape by any means whatsoever.

If a monarch relinquishes the sovereignty, both for himself and for his heirs, his subjects return to the absolute liberty of nature; because, though nature may declare who his sons are, and who are the nearest of his kin, who shall be his heir depends (as was said in the previous chapter) on his own will. If therefore he chooses to have no heir, there is no sovereignty, and no subjection. The case is the same if he dies without known kindred, and without declaration of his heir; for then no heir can be known, and consequently no subjection is due.

If the sovereign banishes his subject, during the banishment that man is not subject. But the man sent on an errand, or given leave to travel, is still subject — though by contract between sovereigns, not by virtue of the covenant of subjection. For whoever enters another's dominion is subject to all the laws of it, unless he has a privilege through the amity of the sovereigns, or by special licence.

If a monarch subdued by war makes himself subject to the victor, his subjects are freed from their former obligation and become obliged to the victor. But if he is held prisoner, or has not the liberty of his own body, he is not understood to have given away the right of sovereignty; and his subjects are therefore obliged to obey the magistrates already in place, who govern not in their own name but in his. For, his right remaining, the question is only one of administration — that is, of the magistrates and officers; and if he has no means to name them, he is presumed to approve those he himself formerly appointed.

title: Chapter 22. Of Systems Subject, Political, and Private
paragraphs: Having spoken of the generation, form, and power of a commonwealth, I am next in order to speak of its parts. And first of systems, which resemble the similar parts, or the muscles, of a natural body. By SYSTEMS I understand any number of men joined in one interest, or in one piece of business. Of these, some are regular and some irregular. Regular are those in which one man, or one assembly of men, is constituted as the representative of the whole number. All others are irregular.

Of regular systems, some are absolute and independent, subject to no one but their own representative — and such are only commonwealths, which I have already spoken of in the five preceding chapters. Others are dependent — that is, subordinate to some sovereign power, to which every one, and also their representative, is subject.

Of subordinate systems, some are political and some private. Political systems (otherwise called bodies politic, or persons in law) are those made by authority from the sovereign power of the commonwealth. Private systems are those constituted by subjects among themselves, or by authority from a foreigner. For no authority derived from a foreign power is, within the dominion of another, public there; it is private.

And of private systems, some are lawful and some unlawful. Lawful are those allowed by the commonwealth; all others are unlawful. Irregular systems are those which, having no representative, consist only in the gathering of people. These, if not forbidden by the commonwealth and not formed for any evil purpose (such as crowds gathering at markets, or shows, or for any other harmless end), are lawful. But when the intention is evil, or (if the number is significant) unknown, they are unlawful.

In bodies politic, the power of the representative is always limited; and what prescribes its limits is the sovereign power. For unlimited power is absolute sovereignty. And the sovereign, in every commonwealth, is the absolute representative of all the subjects; so no other person can be the representative of any part of them except so far as the sovereign gives leave. To give a body politic of subjects leave to have an absolute representative for all intents and purposes would be to abandon that much of the government of the commonwealth, and to divide the dominion, contrary to the subjects' peace and defence — which cannot be understood as the sovereign's intention in any grant that does not plainly and directly discharge them from their subjection. For the inferred consequences of words are not signs of his will when other consequences are signs of the contrary; they are rather signs of error and miscalculation, to which all mankind is too prone.

The bounds of that power which is given to the representative of a body politic are to be noticed from two sources. One is the writ, or letters, from the sovereign; the other is the law of the commonwealth.

For though in the institution or acquisition of a commonwealth, which is independent, there is no need of any written document — because the power of the representative there has no other bounds than those set by the unwritten law of nature — yet in subordinate bodies there are such various limitations necessary about their business, times, and places that they can neither be remembered without letters, nor heeded unless those letters are public — letters patent, that they may be read out to them, and sealed or otherwise marked with the seals or other permanent signs of the sovereign authority.

And because such limitation is not always easy, or perhaps possible, to be set down in writing, the ordinary laws common to all subjects must determine what the representative may lawfully do in all cases where the letters themselves are silent. And therefore —
When the representative is one man, his unauthorised acts are his alone.

In a body politic, if the representative is one man, whatever he does in the person of the body that is not warranted in his letters, nor by the laws, is his own act, and not the act of the body, nor of any other member besides himself. For beyond the limits set by his letters, or by the laws, he represents no man's person but his own. But what he does in keeping with them is the act of every one. For of the sovereign's act every one is the author, because the sovereign is their unlimited representative; and the act of one who does not depart from the sovereign's letters is the sovereign's act, and so every member of the body is the author of it.
When the representative is an assembly, the act binds only those who assented.

But if the representative is an assembly, then whatever that assembly shall decree, when not warranted by their letters or by the laws, is the act of the assembly, or body politic, and the act of every one by whose vote the decree was made — but not the act of any man who, being present, voted against it, nor of any man who was absent, unless he voted by proxy. It is the act of the assembly because it was voted by the majority; and if it is a crime, the assembly may be punished, so far as it is capable — by dissolution, or by forfeiture of their letters (which to such artificial and fictitious bodies amounts to a capital sentence), or (if the assembly has a common stock in which none of the innocent members has property) by a fine. For from corporal penalties nature has exempted all bodies politic. But those who did not give their vote are innocent, because the assembly cannot represent any man in matters unwarranted by their letters, and so the dissenters and absentees are not implicated in their votes.

When the representative is one man, and he borrows money or comes into debt by contract, he alone is liable; the members are not. If the person of a body politic, being in one man, borrows money from a stranger — that is, from one who is not of the same body (no letters need limit borrowing, since it is left to the lender's own inclinations to limit lending) — the debt is the representative's. For if he had authority from his letters to make the members pay what he borrowed, he would in consequence have sovereignty over them; and so the grant would either be void as proceeding from error (a thing commonly incident to human nature), as not being a sufficient sign of the will of the grantor, or, if it were avowed by him, then the representative would be sovereign, and would not fall under the present question (which is only about subordinate bodies). No member is therefore obliged to pay the debt so borrowed; only the representative is. Because the one who lent it, being a stranger to the letters and to the qualifications of the body, takes for his debtors only those who are engaged; and since the representative can engage himself and no one else, the lender has only him for debtor — who must therefore pay him, out of the common stock if there is any, or, if there is none, out of his own estate.
If the representative comes into debt by contract, or by being fined, the case is the same.
When the representative is an assembly, only those who assented are liable.

When the representative is an assembly, and the debt is to a stranger, all those, and only those, are responsible for the debt who gave their votes either to the borrowing of it, or to the contract that made it due, or to the act for which the fine was imposed. For every one of those, by voting, engaged himself for the payment. For he who is the author of the borrowing is obliged to the payment of the whole debt, even though, when paid by any one, the rest are discharged.
If the debt is to one of the assembly, only the body is obliged.

But if the debt is to one of the assembly, the assembly alone is obliged to the payment out of their common stock (if they have any). For having the liberty to vote, if he votes that the money shall be borrowed, he votes that it shall be paid; and if he votes that it shall not be borrowed, or is absent, yet because in lending he votes for the borrowing, he contradicts his earlier vote, and is obliged by the later one, and becomes both borrower and lender. Consequently he cannot demand payment from any particular man, but only from the common treasury; and if that fails, he has no remedy and no complaint, except against himself. Being privy to the assembly's acts and to their means of payment, and not being compelled, he nevertheless, through his own folly, lent his money.

Sometimes lawful; but against sovereign power never. It is plain from this that in bodies politic subordinate, subject to a sovereign power, it is sometimes not only lawful but expedient for a particular man to make open protest against the decrees of the representative assembly, and to have his dissent recorded, or to call witnesses to it; otherwise he may be obliged to pay debts contracted, or be held responsible for crimes committed, by other men. But in a sovereign assembly that liberty is taken away — both because anyone who protests there denies their sovereignty, and because whatever is commanded by the sovereign power is, as far as the subject is concerned (though not always so in the sight of God), justified by the command, since of such command every subject is the author.

The variety of bodies politic is almost infinite. They are distinguished not only by the various affairs for which they are constituted — in which there is an unspeakable diversity — but also by the times, places, and numbers, all subject to many limitations. As to their affairs, some are ordained for government. For instance, the government of a province may be committed to an assembly of men in which all resolutions are to depend on the votes of the majority; and then that assembly is a body politic, and their power is limited by commission. The word 'province' means a charge, or a care of business, which the one whose business it is commits to another man, to be administered for him and under him. So when in one commonwealth there are various countries that have laws distinct from one another, or are far distant in place, and the administration of government is committed to various persons, those countries where the sovereign is not resident, but governs by commission, are called provinces. But of the government of a province by an assembly residing in the province itself there are few examples. The Romans, who had sovereignty over many provinces, governed them always by presidents and praetors, and not by assemblies, as they governed the city of Rome and the territories adjoining. In the same way, when colonies were sent out from England to plant Virginia and the Somers Islands, though the government of them here was committed to assemblies in London, those assemblies never committed the government under them to any assembly in the colony itself, but sent one governor to each plantation. For though every man, where he can be present by nature, wants to share in the government, yet where they cannot be present, men are also inclined by nature to commit the government of their common interest rather to a monarchical than to a popular form of government. This is also evident in those who have great private estates, who, when unwilling to take the trouble of administering the business that belongs to them, choose rather to trust one servant than an assembly of either friends or servants. But however that may be in fact, we may suppose the government of a province, or colony, to be committed to an assembly; and when it is, what I have to say in this place is this: that whatever debt is contracted by that assembly, or whatever unlawful act is decreed, is the act only of those who assented, and not of any who dissented, or were absent, for the reasons already given. Also, that an assembly residing outside the bounds of the colony it governs cannot exercise any power over the persons or goods of any of the colonists, to seize them for debt or other duty, in any place outside the colony itself, as having no jurisdiction or authority elsewhere; the assembly is left to the remedy which the law of the place allows. And though the assembly has the right to impose a fine on any of its members who shall break the laws they make, yet outside the colony itself they have no right to execute the same. And what is said here about the rights of an assembly for the government of a province or a colony applies also to an assembly for the government of a town, or a university, or a college, or a church, or for any other government over the persons of men.

And in general, in all bodies politic, if any particular member considers himself injured by the body itself, the hearing of his case belongs to the sovereign, and to those whom the sovereign has ordained as judges in such cases, or shall ordain for that particular cause — and not to the body itself. For the whole body in this case is his fellow subject. In a sovereign assembly it is otherwise: for there, if the sovereign is not judge (even in his own cause), there can be no judge at all.

In a body politic for the orderly conduct of foreign trade, the most convenient representative is an assembly of all the members — that is, one at which every man who ventures his money may, if he chooses, be present at all the deliberations and resolutions of the body. To prove this, we should consider the end for which men who are merchants — and who can buy and sell, export and import their merchandise according to their own discretion — nevertheless bind themselves up in one corporation. There are indeed few merchants who, with the merchandise they buy at home, can freight a ship to export it, or with that they buy abroad can freight one to bring it home; and so they have need to join together in one society, where every man may either share in the gain in proportion to his venture, or take his own part and sell what he transports or imports at such prices as he thinks fit. But this is no body politic, since there is no common representative to oblige them to any law other than what is common to all other subjects. The end of their incorporating is to make their gain the greater; and this is done in two ways: by sole buying, and by sole selling, both at home and abroad. So to grant to a company of merchants that they shall be a corporation, or body politic, is to grant them a double monopoly — to be sole buyers, and to be sole sellers. For when there is a company incorporated for any particular foreign country, only its members export the commodities that are saleable in that country; which is sole buying at home and sole selling abroad. At home there is only one buyer, and abroad only one seller: both of which are gainful to the merchant, because by this means they buy at home at lower, and sell abroad at higher, rates. And abroad there is only one buyer of foreign merchandise, and only one seller of it at home: both of which, again, are gainful to the venturers.

Of this double monopoly, one part is disadvantageous to the people at home, the other to foreigners. At home, by their sole right of exporting, they set what price they please on the husbandry and handiwork of the people; and by sole importing, what price they please on all foreign commodities the people need. Both of these are bad for the people. On the other side, by sole selling of native commodities abroad, and sole buying of foreign commodities on the spot, they raise the price of the latter and beat down the price of the former, to the disadvantage of the foreigner: for where there is only one seller, the goods are dearer, and where only one buyer, cheaper. Such corporations therefore are nothing but monopolies — though they would be very profitable for a commonwealth if, being bound up in one body in foreign markets, they were at home left at liberty, every man to buy and sell at whatever price he could.

Since then the end of these bodies of merchants is not a common benefit to the whole body (which in this case has no common stock except what is deducted from each member's particular venture, for building, buying, victualling, and manning ships), but the particular gain of every venturer, it is reasonable that every man should be familiar with the use to which his own money is put — that is, that every one should be part of the assembly that has the power to direct it, and have access to the accounts. So the representative of such a body must be an assembly, at which every member of the body may, if he wishes, be present at the consultations.

If a body politic of merchants contracts a debt to a stranger by the act of their representative assembly, every member is liable individually for the whole. For a stranger can take no notice of their private laws, but regards them as so many particular men, every one obliged to the whole payment, until payment made by one discharges all the rest. But if the debt is to one of the company, the creditor is debtor for the whole to himself, and cannot therefore demand his debt except from the common stock, if there is any.

If the commonwealth lays a tax on the body, it is understood to be laid on every member in proportion to his particular venture in the company. For there is in this case no other common stock than what is made up of their particular ventures.

If a fine is laid on the body for some unlawful act, those alone are liable by whose votes the act was decreed, or by whose assistance it was carried out; for in none of the rest is there any crime except being of the body — and that, if it is a crime (since the body was ordained by the authority of the commonwealth), is not his.

If one of the members is indebted to the body, he may be sued by the body; but his goods cannot be taken, nor his person imprisoned, by the authority of the body — only by the authority of the commonwealth. For if they could do it by their own authority, they could by their own authority give judgement that the debt is due, which is as much as to be judge in their own cause.

These bodies, formed for the government of men or for trade, are either perpetual or for a time prescribed in writing. But there are also bodies whose duration is limited only by the nature of their business. For example, if a sovereign monarch, or a sovereign assembly, thinks fit to command the towns and other parts of his territory to send him their deputies, to inform him of the condition and necessities of the subjects, or to advise with him for the making of good laws, or for any other cause, as with one person representing the whole country, such deputies, having a place and time of meeting assigned to them, are there, and at that time, a body politic, representing every subject of that dominion — but only for such matters as are put to them by the man, or assembly, who by the sovereign authority sent for them. And when it is declared that no more shall be put to them, or debated by them, the body is dissolved. For if they were the absolute representative of the people, they would be the sovereign assembly; and so there would be two sovereign assemblies, or two sovereigns, over the same people — which is incompatible with their peace. And so where there is once a sovereignty, there can be no absolute representation of the people but by it. As for the limits of how far such a body shall represent the whole people, those are set out in the writing by which they were sent for. For the people cannot choose their deputies to any other intent than is expressed in the writing directed to them from their sovereign.

Private bodies that are regular and lawful are those constituted without letters, or any other written authority, beyond the laws common to all other subjects. And because they are united in one person representative, they are held to be regular. Such are all families, in which the father, or master, orders the whole family. For he binds his children and servants, as far as the law permits, though not further — since none of them are bound to obedience in actions the law has forbidden to be done. In all other actions, while they are under domestic government, they are subject to their fathers and masters, as to their immediate sovereigns. For the father and master, being before the institution of the commonwealth absolute sovereigns in their own families, lose afterwards no more of their authority than the law of the commonwealth takes from them.

Private bodies regular but unlawful are those that unite themselves into one representative person without any public authority at all — such as the corporations of beggars, thieves, and gypsies, the better to organise their trade of begging and stealing; and the corporations of men who, by authority from any foreign person, unite themselves in another's dominion, for the easier propagation of doctrines, and for forming a party against the power of the commonwealth.

Irregular systems, being in their nature only leagues, or sometimes mere gatherings of people without union to any particular design, not held together by obligation of one to another but proceeding only from a similarity of wills and inclinations, become lawful or unlawful according to the lawfulness or unlawfulness of each particular man's design in them; and his design is to be understood from the occasion.

Leagues among subjects (since leagues are commonly made for mutual defence) are, in a commonwealth (which is itself nothing more than a league of all the subjects together), for the most part unnecessary, and smack of unlawful design; and are for that reason unlawful, and commonly go under the name of factions, or conspiracies. For a league, being a connection of men by covenant, if there is no power given to any one man or assembly (as in the condition of mere nature) to compel performance, is valid only so long as no just cause of distrust arises. So leagues between commonwealths, over which no human power is established to keep them all in awe, are not only lawful but also profitable for as long as they last. But leagues among the subjects of one and the same commonwealth, where everyone may obtain his right by means of the sovereign power, are unnecessary for the maintaining of peace and justice — and (if the design of them is evil, or unknown to the commonwealth) unlawful. For all united strength among private men is, if for an evil intent, unjust; if for intent unknown, dangerous to the public, and unjustly concealed.

If the sovereign power is in a great assembly, and a number of men, who are part of that assembly, consult apart without authority, to contrive the guidance of the rest, this is a faction, or unlawful conspiracy — being a fraudulent leading of the assembly for their own particular interest. But if a man whose private interest is to be debated and judged in the assembly makes as many friends as he can, in him it is no injustice; in this case he is no part of the assembly. And though he hire such friends with money (unless there is an express law against it), it is still not injustice. For sometimes (such are men's manners) justice cannot be had without money; and every man may think his own cause just until it is heard and judged.

In all commonwealths, if a private man keeps more servants than the government of his estate, and the lawful employment he has for them, requires, it is faction, and unlawful. Having the protection of the commonwealth, he has no need of the defence of private force. And whereas in nations not thoroughly civilised, several great families have lived in continual hostility, and have invaded one another by private force, it is plain enough that they have acted unjustly — or else that they had no commonwealth.

And as factions for kindred, so also factions for the government of religion — as of Papists, Protestants, and so on — or for the form of the state — as Patricians and Plebeians in old time at Rome, and Aristocraticals and Democraticals in old time in Greece — are unjust, as being contrary to the peace and safety of the people, and a taking of the sword out of the hand of the sovereign.

A gathering of people is an irregular system, whose lawfulness or unlawfulness depends on the occasion, and on the number of those assembled. If the occasion is lawful and clear, the gathering is lawful, as in the usual meeting of men at church, or at a public show, in the usual numbers. For if the numbers are extraordinarily great, the occasion is not evident; and consequently he who cannot give a particular and good account of his being among them is to be judged conscious of an unlawful and tumultuous design. It may be lawful for a thousand men to join in a petition to be delivered to a judge or magistrate; yet if a thousand men come to present it, it is a tumultuous assembly, because there need only be one or two for that purpose. But in such cases as these, it is not a fixed number that makes the assembly unlawful, but a number such that the officers on the spot are not able to suppress it and bring it to justice.

When an unusual number of men gather against a man whom they accuse, the assembly is an unlawful tumult, because they could deliver their accusation to the magistrate by a few, or by one man. Such was the case of St Paul at Ephesus, where Demetrius and a great number of other men brought two of Paul's companions before the magistrate, saying with one voice, 'Great is Diana of the Ephesians' — which was their way of demanding justice against them for teaching the people doctrine contrary to their religion and to their trade. The occasion here, considering the laws of that people, was just; and yet their assembly was judged unlawful, and the magistrate rebuked them for it in these words (Acts 19:40): 'If Demetrius and the other workmen can accuse any man of anything, there are pleas, and deputies; let them accuse one another. And if you have any other matter to demand, your case may be judged in a lawfully called assembly. For we are in danger of being accused for this day's sedition, because there is no cause by which any man can give any reason for this concourse of people.' There he calls an assembly of which men can give no just account a sedition, and one for which they could not answer. And this is all I shall say about systems and assemblies of people, which (as I said) may be compared to the similar parts of a man's body: those that are lawful, to the muscles; those that are unlawful, to wens, boils, and abscesses, bred by the unnatural inflowing of evil humours.

title: Chapter 23. Of the Public Ministers of Sovereign Power
paragraphs: In the last chapter I spoke of the similar parts of a commonwealth; in this I shall speak of the organic parts — namely, the public ministers.

A PUBLIC MINISTER is one who, by the sovereign (whether a monarch or an assembly), is employed in any affair with authority to represent in that employment the person of the commonwealth. Now since every man, or assembly, that has sovereignty represents two persons — or (as it is more commonly put) has two capacities, one natural and one political — a monarch having the person not only of the commonwealth but also of a man, and a sovereign assembly having the person not only of the commonwealth but also of the assembly — those who serve them in their natural capacity are not public ministers; only those who serve them in the administration of the public business are. So neither ushers, nor sergeants, nor any other officers who wait on the assembly for no other purpose than the convenience of the men assembled, in an aristocracy or a democracy, nor stewards, chamberlains, cofferers, nor any other officers of a monarch's household, are public ministers in a monarchy.

Of public ministers, some have charge committed to them of a general administration, either of the whole dominion or of a part of it. Of the whole: as when a Protector or Regent may be entrusted by the predecessor of an infant king, during his minority, with the whole administration of his kingdom. In that case, every subject is obliged to obedience so far as the ordinances the Protector makes, and the commands he gives, are in the king's name and not inconsistent with his sovereign power. Of a part, or province: as when either a monarch or a sovereign assembly gives the general charge of it to a governor, lieutenant, prefect, or viceroy. In this case too, every member of that province is obliged to all that the deputy shall do in the name of the sovereign, provided it is not incompatible with the sovereign's right. For such Protectors, viceroys, and governors have no right except what depends on the sovereign's will; and no commission given to them can be interpreted as a declaration of his will to transfer the sovereignty unless that intention is in express and clear words. This kind of public minister resembles the nerves and tendons that move the various limbs of a natural body.

Others have a special administration — that is, charge of some particular business, either at home or abroad. At home, first, for the economy of the commonwealth: those who have authority over the public treasure — tributes, impositions, rents, fines, or any other public revenue — to collect, receive, disburse, or audit it, are public ministers. Ministers, because they serve the representative person and can do nothing against his command, or without his authority; public, because they serve him in his political capacity.

Second, those who have authority over the militia — to have custody of arms, forts, and ports; to levy, pay, or lead soldiers; or to provide anything necessary for the conduct of war by land or sea — are public ministers. But a soldier without command, though he fights for the commonwealth, does not for that reason represent its person, because there is no one for him to represent it to. Everyone with a command represents the commonwealth only to those whom he commands.

Those also who have authority to teach, or to enable others to teach, the people their duty to the sovereign power, and to instruct them in the knowledge of what is just and unjust — thereby fitting them better to live in godliness and in peace among themselves, and to resist the public enemy — are public ministers. Ministers, in that they do this not by their own authority but by another's; and public, because they do it (or should do it) by no authority but the sovereign's. The monarch, or the sovereign assembly, alone has direct authority from God to teach and instruct the people; and no one but the sovereign receives his power Dei Gratia in the simple sense — that is, from the favour of God alone. All others receive theirs from the favour and providence of God and of their sovereign: in a monarchy, Dei Gratia et Regis, or Dei Providentia et Voluntate Regis.

Those also to whom jurisdiction is given are public ministers. For in their seats of justice they represent the person of the sovereign, and their sentence is his sentence. For (as was declared before) all judicature is essentially annexed to the sovereignty, and so all other judges are only ministers of him, or them, who holds the sovereign power. And as controversies are of two sorts — namely, of fact and of law — so are judgements: some of fact, some of law. So in the same controversy there may be two judges, one of fact, the other of law.

In both these kinds of controversy, a further controversy may arise between the party being judged and the judge himself; and because they are both subjects to the sovereign, this should in equity be judged by men agreed on by the consent of both — for no man can be a judge in his own case. But the sovereign is already agreed on as judge by them both, and so is either to hear the case and decide it himself, or to appoint as judges such men as they both agree on. And this agreement is understood to be made between them in various ways. First, if the defendant is allowed to challenge those of his judges whose interest makes him suspect them (since the complainant has already chosen his own judge), then those he does not challenge are judges he himself agrees on. Second, if he appeals to any other judge, he can appeal no further; his appeal is his choice. Third, if he appeals to the sovereign himself, and the sovereign — either in person, or by delegates the parties shall agree on — gives sentence, that sentence is final; for the defendant is judged by his own judges, that is, by himself.

Considering these properties of just and rational judicature, I cannot help observing the excellent constitution of the courts of justice established in England both for Common Pleas and for Public Pleas. By Common Pleas I mean those in which both the complainant and the defendant are subjects; and by Public Pleas (which are also called Pleas of the Crown) those in which the complainant is the sovereign. Whereas there were two orders of men, one being lords and the other commons, the lords had the privilege of having for their judges in all capital crimes none but lords, and as many of them as would be present — which, being always acknowledged as a privilege of favour, meant their judges were none but those they themselves had wanted. In all controversies, every subject (and likewise the lords in civil controversies) had as judges men of the county where the matter in dispute lay; against whom he could make his challenges, until at last twelve men without challenge were agreed on, and he was judged by those twelve. So having his own judges, the party could allege nothing to keep the sentence from being final. These public persons, with authority from the sovereign power either to instruct or to judge the people, are members of the commonwealth that may fitly be compared to the organs of voice in a natural body.

Public ministers are also all those who have authority from the sovereign to procure the execution of judgements given, to publish the sovereign's commands, to suppress tumults, to apprehend and imprison wrongdoers, and to perform other acts tending to the preservation of peace. For every act they do by such authority is the act of the commonwealth; and their service answers to that of the hands in a natural body.

Public ministers abroad are those who represent the person of their own sovereign to foreign states. Such are ambassadors, messengers, agents, and heralds, sent by public authority and on public business.

But those who are sent by the authority only of some private party of a troubled state, though they are received, are neither public nor private ministers of the commonwealth, because none of their actions have the commonwealth for their author. Likewise, an ambassador sent from a prince to congratulate, condole with, or attend a ceremony — though the authority is public, since the business is private, belonging to the prince in his natural capacity — is a private person. Also if a man is sent into another country to explore their counsels and strength in secret, though both the authority and the business are public, since there is no person in him to be acknowledged but his own, he is only a private minister; but a minister of the commonwealth still, and may be compared to an eye in the natural body. And those who are appointed to receive the petitions or other information of the people, and are as it were the public ear, are public ministers, and represent their sovereign in that office.

Neither a counsellor, nor a council of state, if we consider it as having no authority of judicature or command, but only of giving advice to the sovereign when it is requested, or of offering it unrequested, is a public person. For the advice is addressed to the sovereign alone, whose person cannot in his own presence be represented to him by another. But a body of counsellors is never without some other authority, either of judicature or of immediate administration. In a monarchy, they represent the monarch in delivering his commands to the public ministers. In a democracy, the council, or senate, sets the result of its deliberations before the people as a council; but when it appoints judges, hears cases, or gives audience to ambassadors, it acts in the capacity of a minister of the people. In an aristocracy, the council of state is the sovereign assembly itself, and gives counsel to no one but themselves.

title: Chapter 24. Of the Nutrition, and Procreation of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: The NUTRITION of a commonwealth consists in the plenty and distribution of the materials that sustain life; in their concoction, or preparation; and (once prepared) in their conveyance, by suitable conduits, to public use.

As for the plenty of matter, it is a thing limited by nature to those commodities which God, from the two breasts of our common mother — land and sea — either gives freely to mankind or sells to it for labour.

For the matter of this nourishment, consisting in animals, vegetables, and minerals, God has laid them freely before us, on or near the face of the earth; so that nothing more is needed than the labour and industry of gathering them in. Plenty therefore depends (next to God's favour) simply on the labour and industry of men.

This matter, commonly called commodities, is partly native and partly foreign — native being what is to be had within the territory of the commonwealth, foreign being what is imported from outside. And because there is no territory under the dominion of one commonwealth (except one of very vast extent) that produces all things needful for the maintenance and motion of the whole body, and few that do not produce something more than necessary, the surplus commodities within can cease to be surplus by being used to supply needs at home, in return for things to be had abroad — whether by exchange, by just war, or by labour. For a man's labour is also a commodity, exchangeable for benefit as much as anything else. And there have been commonwealths which, with no more territory than served them for habitation, have nevertheless not only maintained but also increased their power, partly by the labour of trading from one place to another, and partly by selling manufactures whose raw materials were brought in from other places.

The distribution of the materials of this nourishment is the constitution of mine, thine, and his — in one word, property; and in every kind of commonwealth it belongs to the sovereign power. For where there is no commonwealth, there is (as has already been shown) a perpetual war of every man against his neighbour; so everything is his who can get it and keep it by force — which is neither property nor community, but uncertainty. This is so evident that even Cicero (a passionate defender of liberty), in a public pleading, attributes all property to the civil law: 'Let the civil law,' he says, 'be once abandoned, or even negligently guarded — not to say oppressed — and there is nothing that any man can be sure to receive from his ancestor, or to leave to his children.' And again: 'Take away the civil law, and no man knows what is his own and what is another's.' Since therefore the introduction of property is an effect of the commonwealth, which can do nothing except by the person who represents it, it is the act of the sovereign alone; and it consists in the laws, which none can make who do not have the sovereign power.
