And those who have a multitude of powerful kinsmen, and popular men who have gained a reputation among the multitude, take courage to violate the laws from a hope of overpowering the authority to whom it belongs to put the laws into execution.

And those who have a great, false opinion of their own wisdom take upon themselves to criticise the actions, and call in question the authority, of those who govern; and so to unsettle the laws with their public discourse, that nothing shall be a crime but what their own designs require should be so. The same men are prone to all the crimes that consist in craft, and in the deceiving of their neighbours, because they think their designs too subtle to be perceived. These, I say, are effects of a false presumption of their own wisdom. For of those who are the first movers in the disturbance of a commonwealth (which can never happen without a civil war), very few are left alive long enough to see their new designs established; so that the benefit of their crimes accrues to posterity, and to such as would have least wished it — which argues they were not as wise as they thought. And those who deceive on the hope of not being noticed commonly deceive themselves (the darkness in which they believe they lie hidden being nothing but their own blindness), and are no wiser than children who think everything hidden by hiding their own eyes.

And generally all vainglorious men (unless they are also timorous) are subject to anger, being more prone than others to interpret as contempt the ordinary liberty of conversation. And there are few crimes that may not be produced by anger.

As for the passions of hate, lust, ambition, and covetousness — what crimes they tend to produce is so obvious to every man's experience and understanding that nothing needs to be said of them, except that they are infirmities so annexed to the nature both of man and of every other living creature that their effects cannot be prevented except by extraordinary use of reason, or by constant severity in punishing them. For in the things men hate they find a continual and unavoidable molestation; and so either a man's patience must be everlasting, or he must be eased by removing the power of that which molests him. The former is difficult; the latter is many times impossible without some violation of the law. Ambition and covetousness too are passions perpetually present, and pressing, whereas reason is not perpetually on hand to resist them; and so whenever the hope of impunity appears, their effects follow. As for lust, what it lacks in lasting it makes up for in vehemence — which is enough to outweigh the apprehension of any easy or uncertain punishments.
Fear is sometimes the cause of crime, as when the danger is neither present nor bodily.

Of all the passions, the one that least inclines men to break the laws is fear. Indeed (with some exceptions in generous natures) it is the only thing — when there is the appearance of profit or pleasure from breaking the laws — that makes men keep them. And yet in many cases a crime may be committed through fear.

For not every fear justifies the action it produces, but only the fear of bodily hurt — what we call bodily fear — from which a man cannot see how to be delivered except by the action. A man is assaulted, fears immediate death, from which he sees no escape except by wounding the one assaulting him; if he wounds him to death, this is no crime. For no man is supposed at the making of a commonwealth to have abandoned the defence of his life or his limbs, where the law cannot arrive in time to help him. But to kill a man because from his actions or his threats I may argue that he will kill me when he can (when I have the time and means to demand protection from the sovereign power) is a crime. Again, a man receives words of disgrace, or some little injury (for which the makers of the laws have assigned no punishment, nor thought it worthy of a man with the use of reason to take notice of); and he is afraid that, unless he avenges it, he will fall into contempt, and consequently be exposed to similar injuries from others. To avoid this he breaks the law, and protects himself for the future by the terror of his private revenge. This is a crime. For the hurt is not bodily but imagined; and though in this corner of the world made tangible by a custom not many years since begun, among young and vain men, it is so light that a gallant man, and one assured of his own courage, can take no notice of it. Also, a man may stand in fear of spirits, either through his own superstition or through too much credit given to other men who tell him of strange dreams and visions, and may be made to believe they will hurt him for doing or omitting various things — even when doing or omitting them is contrary to the laws. What is done, or omitted, on such fear is not excused by it; it is a crime. For (as I have shown before, in the second chapter) dreams are naturally only the fancies remaining in sleep after the impressions our senses had previously received while waking; and when men are by some accident unsure whether they have slept, the dreams seem to be real visions. And so the man who presumes to break the law on his own, or another's, dream, or pretended vision, or on any other fancy about the power of invisible spirits beyond what the commonwealth permits, leaves the law of nature, which is a certain offence, and follows the imagery of his own or another private man's brain — about which he can never know whether it signifies anything or nothing, nor whether the one who tells his dream is speaking the truth or lying. If every private man were to be allowed to do this (as they all must, by the law of nature, if any one is), no law could be made to hold, and the whole commonwealth would be dissolved.

From these different sources of crimes, it already appears that all crimes are not (as the Stoics of old maintained) of the same alloy. There is room not only for EXCUSE, by which what seemed a crime is proved to be none at all, but also for EXTENUATION, by which the crime that seemed great is made less. For though all crimes equally deserve the name of injustice, as all deviation from a straight line is equally crookedness (which the Stoics rightly observed), it does not follow that all crimes are equally unjust, any more than that all crooked lines are equally crooked — which the Stoics, not observing, held it as great a crime to kill a hen against the law as to kill one's father.

What totally excuses an act, and takes away from it the nature of a crime, can be only what at the same time takes away the obligation of the law. For an act committed against a law to which the doer is obliged can be nothing but a crime.

Lack of means to know the law totally excuses; for a law of which a man has no means to inform himself is not binding. But lack of diligence to inquire is not to be reckoned a lack of means; nor shall any man who claims reason enough for the government of his own affairs be supposed to lack the means of knowing the laws of nature, because they are known by the reason he claims. Only children and madmen are excused from offences against the natural law.

Where a man is a captive, or in the power of the enemy (and he is in the power of the enemy when his person, or his means of living, is so), if it is through no fault of his own, the obligation of the law ceases; because he must either obey the enemy or die, and consequently such obedience is no crime. For no man is obliged (when the protection of the law fails) not to protect himself by the best means he can.

If a man, by the terror of immediate death, is compelled to do an act against the law, he is totally excused; because no law can oblige a man to abandon his own preservation. And even supposing such a law were obligatory, a man would still reason thus: 'If I do not do it, I die now; if I do it, I die later; therefore by doing it, I gain time of life.' Nature therefore compels him to the act.

When a man is destitute of food, or of any other thing necessary for his life, and cannot preserve himself except by some act against the law — as if in a great famine he takes by force or stealth the food he cannot obtain for money or charity, or in defence of his life snatches away another man's sword — he is totally excused, for the reason just given.

Again, acts done against the law by the authority of another are by that authority excused, as against the author; for no man ought to condemn his own act done by another, who is only his instrument. But it is not excused as against a third person thereby injured; for in the violation of the law both the author and the actor are criminals. From this it follows that when the man, or assembly, that has the sovereign power commands a man to do what is contrary to a previous law, the doing of it is totally excused. For the sovereign ought not to condemn it himself, since he is the author; and what cannot justly be condemned by the sovereign cannot justly be punished by anyone else. Besides, when the sovereign commands anything to be done contrary to his own previous law, the command is, as to that particular act, an abrogation of the law.

If the man, or assembly, that has the sovereign power disclaims any right essential to the sovereignty — by which there accrues to the subject any liberty inconsistent with the sovereign power, that is, with the very being of a commonwealth — then if the subject refuses to obey the command in anything contrary to the liberty granted, this is nevertheless a sin, and contrary to the duty of the subject; for he ought to take notice of what is inconsistent with the sovereignty, since the sovereignty was erected by his own consent and for his own defence, and such liberty as is inconsistent with it was granted through ignorance of the evil consequences. But if he not only disobeys but also resists a public minister in the execution of it, then it is a crime; because he could have been righted, without any breach of the peace, by complaint.

The degrees of crime are taken on various scales, and measured: first, by the malignity of the source or cause; second, by the contagion of the example; third, by the mischief of the effect; and fourth, by the concurrence of times, places, and persons.

The same act done against the law, if it proceeds from presumption of strength, riches, or friends to resist those who are to execute the law, is a greater crime than if it proceeds from the hope of not being discovered, or of escape by flight. For presumption of impunity by force is a root from which springs, at all times and on every temptation, a contempt of all laws; whereas in the latter case, the apprehension of danger that makes a man flee renders him more obedient for the future. A crime that we know to be a crime is greater than the same crime proceeding from a false belief that it is lawful. For the man who commits it against his own conscience presumes on his force, or on some other power, which encourages him to commit the same again; but he who does it through error, once the error has been shown to him, conforms to the law.

He whose error proceeds from the authority of a teacher, or an interpreter of the law publicly authorised, is not as much at fault as he whose error proceeds from a stubborn pursuit of his own principles and reasoning. For what is taught by one who teaches by public authority is taught by the commonwealth, and has a resemblance of law until the same authority controls it. In all crimes that do not contain a denial of the sovereign power, and are not against an evident law, this totally excuses; whereas the man who grounds his actions on his private judgement ought, according to the rightness or the error of it, to stand or to fall.

The same act is a greater crime if it has been consistently punished in other men than if there have been many precedent examples of impunity. For those examples are so many hopes of impunity given by the sovereign himself; and because the one who furnishes a man with such a hope and presumption of mercy as encourages him to offend has his part in the offence, he cannot reasonably charge the offender with the whole.

A crime arising from a sudden passion is not so great as when the same arises from long deliberation. For in the former case there is room for extenuation, in the common infirmity of human nature; but he who does it with premeditation has used circumspection, and cast his eye on the law, on the punishment, and on its consequences for human society — all of which he, in committing the crime, has despised and ranked beneath his own appetite. But no suddenness of passion is sufficient for a total excuse; for all the time between the first knowing of the law and the commission of the act shall be reckoned as time for deliberation, since he ought to rectify the irregularity of his passions by meditation on the law.

Where the law is publicly, and with diligence, read and interpreted before all the people, an act done against it is a greater crime than where men are left without such instruction, and have to inquire about it with difficulty, uncertainty, and interruption of their callings, and to be informed by private men. For in the latter case, part of the fault is discharged on common infirmity; in the former case there is apparent negligence, which is not without some contempt of the sovereign power.

Acts which the law expressly condemns, but which the lawmaker by other plain signs of his will tacitly approves, are lesser crimes than the same acts condemned both by the law and by the lawmaker. For since the will of the lawmaker is law, there appear in this case two contradictory laws, which would totally excuse if men were bound to take notice of the sovereign's approval by arguments other than what is expressed by his command. But because punishments follow not only from the transgression of his law but also from the keeping of it, he is in part a cause of the transgression, and so cannot reasonably impute the whole crime to the wrongdoer. For example: the law condemns duels; the punishment is made capital. On the other hand, the man who refuses a duel is subject to contempt and scorn, with no remedy; and sometimes he is thought by the sovereign himself unworthy to have any charge or preferment in war. If on this account he accepts a duel — considering that all men lawfully try to obtain the good opinion of those who have sovereign power — he ought not in reason to be rigorously punished, since part of the fault may be discharged on the punisher. I say this, not as wishing for the liberty of private revenges or any other kind of disobedience, but as urging care in governors not to countenance obliquely anything they directly forbid. The examples of princes, to those who see them, are, and ever have been, more powerful to govern men's actions than the laws themselves. And though it is our duty to do, not what they do, but what they say, that duty will never be performed until it pleases God to give men an extraordinary and supernatural grace to follow that precept.

Again, if we compare crimes by the mischief of their effects: first, the same act, when it extends to the damage of many, is a greater crime than when it extends only to the hurt of few. And so when an act hurts not only in the present, but also (by example) in the future, it is a greater crime than if it hurts only in the present. For the former is a fertile crime, and multiplies to the hurt of many; the latter is barren. To maintain doctrines contrary to the religion established in the commonwealth is a greater fault in an authorised preacher than in a private person; so also is it to live profanely, intemperately, or to do any irreligious act whatever. Likewise, in a professor of law, to maintain any point, or do any act, that tends to the weakening of the sovereign power is a greater crime than in another man. Also, in a man whose reputation for wisdom is such that his counsels are followed, or his actions imitated, by many, his act against the law is a greater crime than the same act in another man. For such men not only commit a crime, but teach it as law to all other men. And in general, all crimes are the greater for the scandal they give; that is, for becoming stumbling-blocks to the weak, who look not so much at the way they go in as at the light that other men carry before them.

Also, acts of hostility against the present state of the commonwealth are greater crimes than the same acts done against private men; for the damage extends itself to all. Such are the betraying of the strengths, or the revealing of the secrets, of the commonwealth to an enemy; also all attempts on the representative of the commonwealth, whether a monarch or an assembly; and all endeavours by word or deed to diminish the authority of the same, either at the present time or in the succession. These crimes the Latins understand by Crimina Laesae Majestatis, and consist in design, or act, contrary to a fundamental law.

Likewise, those crimes which render judgements of no effect are greater crimes than injuries done to one or a few persons — as taking money to give a false judgement or false testimony is a greater crime than otherwise to defraud a man of the same, or a greater, sum. For not only does the man suffer who falls by such judgements; all judgements are rendered useless, and occasion is given to force and private revenges.
Also robbery and embezzlement of the public treasure or revenues is a greater crime than the robbing or defrauding of a private man — because to rob the public is to rob many at once.

Likewise, the counterfeit usurpation of public ministry, the counterfeiting of public seals, or of public coin, is greater than counterfeiting a private man's person or seal; because the fraud extends to the damage of many.
Of acts against the law done against private men, the greater crime is the one in which the damage, in the common opinion of men, is most keenly felt. And so —
To kill against the law is a greater crime than any other injury, life preserved.
And to kill with torment is greater than simply to kill.
And the mutilation of a limb is greater than the spoiling a man of his goods.
And the spoiling a man of his goods by terror of death or wounds is greater than by clandestine surreption.
And by clandestine surreption is greater than by consent fraudulently obtained.
And the violation of chastity by force is greater than by flattery.
And the violation of a married woman is greater than of an unmarried one.
For all these things are commonly so valued — though some men are more, and some less, sensitive to the same offence. But the law regards not the particular but the general inclination of mankind.

And so the offence men take from contumely in words or gesture, when these produce no other harm than the present grief of the man reproached, has been ignored in the laws of the Greeks, Romans, and other commonwealths both ancient and modern; supposing the true cause of such grief to consist not in the contumely (which takes no hold on men aware of their own virtue), but in the pusillanimity of the man offended by it.

Also, a crime against a private man is much aggravated by the person, time, and place. For to kill one's parent is a greater crime than to kill another; for the parent ought to have the honour of a sovereign (though he has surrendered his power to the civil law), because he had it originally by nature. And to rob a poor man is a greater crime than to rob a rich man, because to the poor man the damage is more keenly felt.
And a crime committed in the time or place appointed for devotion is greater than if committed at another time or place; for it proceeds from a greater contempt of the law.
Many other cases of aggravation and extenuation might be added; but by the ones I have set down, it is obvious to every man how to take the measure of any other crime proposed.

Finally, because in almost all crimes there is an injury done not only to some private man but also to the commonwealth, the same crime, when the accusation is in the name of the commonwealth, is called a public crime, and when in the name of a private man, a private crime. The pleas accordingly are called public — judicia publica, Pleas of the Crown — or private. So in an accusation of murder, if the accuser is a private man, the plea is a private plea; if the accuser is the sovereign, the plea is a public plea.

title: Chapter 28. Of Punishments, and Rewards
paragraphs: 'A PUNISHMENT is an evil inflicted by public authority on the man who has done, or omitted, what is judged by the same authority to be a transgression of the law, to the end that the will of men may thereby be the better disposed to obedience.'

Before I infer anything from this definition, there is a question of great importance to be answered: by what door did the right, or authority, of punishing in any case come in? For by what has been said before, no man is supposed to be bound by covenant not to resist violence; and consequently it cannot be supposed that he gave any right to another to lay violent hands on his person. In the making of a commonwealth, every man gives away the right of defending another, but not of defending himself. He also obliges himself to assist the holder of the sovereignty in the punishing of another, but not of himself. But to covenant to assist the sovereign in doing harm to another — unless the man so covenanting has a right to do it himself — is not to give the sovereign a right to punish. It is therefore plain that the right which the commonwealth (that is, the man or men representing it) has to punish is not grounded on any concession or gift from the subjects. But I have also shown before that, before the institution of the commonwealth, every man had a right to every thing, and to do whatever he thought necessary for his own preservation — subduing, hurting, or killing any man to that end. And this is the foundation of that right of punishing exercised in every commonwealth. For the subjects did not give the sovereign that right; only, by laying down their own, they strengthened him to use his own, as he should think fit, for the preservation of them all. So that the right of punishing was not given to him, but left to him, and to him alone; and (except for the limits set by natural law) it is as entire as it was in the condition of mere nature, and of war of every one against his neighbour.
From the definition of punishment, I infer, first, that neither private revenges nor injuries by private men can properly be called punishment, because they do not proceed from public authority.
Second, that to be neglected, and not promoted, by the public favour is not a punishment, because no new evil is thereby inflicted on any man; he is only left in the state he was in before.

Third, that an evil inflicted by public authority, without prior public condemnation, is not to be called by the name of punishment but of a hostile act; because the act for which a man is punished ought first to be judged by public authority to be a transgression of the law.

Fourth, that an evil inflicted by usurped power, and by judges without authority from the sovereign, is not punishment but an act of hostility; because the acts of usurped power do not have for their author the person condemned, and so are not acts of public authority.

Fifth, that all evil inflicted without intention, or possibility, of disposing the wrongdoer — or (by his example) other men — to obey the laws, is not punishment, but an act of hostility; because without such an end, no hurt done falls under that name.

Sixth, whereas to certain actions there are annexed by nature various hurtful consequences — as when a man, in assaulting another, is himself slain or wounded, or when he falls sick through the doing of some unlawful act — such hurt, though in respect of God (who is the author of nature) may be said to be inflicted, and so a divine punishment, is not contained in the name of punishment in respect of men, because it is not inflicted by the authority of man.
Hurt inflicted, if less than the benefit of transgressing, is not punishment.

Seventh, if the harm inflicted is less than the benefit, or contentment, that naturally follows the crime committed, that harm is not within the definition; it is rather the price, or redemption, than the punishment of a crime. For it belongs to the nature of punishment to have for its end the disposing of men to obey the law — an end which (if it is less than the benefit of transgression) it does not attain, but works the contrary effect.
Where the punishment is annexed to the law, a greater hurt is not punishment but hostility.

Eighth, if a punishment is determined and prescribed in the law itself, and after the crime is committed a greater punishment is inflicted, the excess is not punishment but an act of hostility. For since the aim of punishment is not revenge but terror, and the terror of a great unknown punishment is taken away by the declaration of a lesser one, the unexpected addition is no part of the punishment. But where no punishment at all is determined by the law, then whatever is inflicted has the nature of punishment. For the man who goes about violating a law in which no penalty is determined expects an indeterminate — that is, an arbitrary — punishment.

Ninth, harm inflicted for an act done before there was a law that forbade it is not punishment but an act of hostility. For before the law, there is no transgression of the law; but punishment supposes an act judged to have been a transgression of the law. Therefore harm inflicted before the law was made is not punishment but an act of hostility.

Tenth, hurt inflicted on the representative of the commonwealth is not punishment but an act of hostility, because it belongs to the nature of punishment to be inflicted by public authority — which is the authority only of the representative itself.

Lastly, harm inflicted on one who is a declared enemy does not fall under the name of punishment. For seeing that they were either never subject to the law, and therefore cannot transgress it, or, having been subject to it, profess to be no longer so and consequently deny that they can transgress it, all the harms that can be done to them must be taken as acts of hostility. And in declared hostility, all infliction of evil is lawful. From which it follows that if a subject by act or word knowingly and deliberately denies the authority of the representative of the commonwealth, then (whatever penalty has formerly been ordained for treason) he may lawfully be made to suffer whatever the representative will. For in denying subjection, he denies such punishment as has been ordained by law, and so suffers as an enemy of the commonwealth — that is, according to the will of the representative. For the punishments set down in the law are for subjects, not for enemies; such as are those who, having by their own act been subjects, deliberately revolt and deny the sovereign power.
The first, and most general, division of punishments is into divine and human. Of the divine I shall have occasion to speak in a more suitable place hereafter.
Human punishments are those inflicted by the command of man, and are either corporal, financial, ignominious, imprisonment, exile, or some mixture of these.

Corporal punishment is that which is inflicted on the body directly, and according to the intention of the one inflicting it — such as stripes, wounds, or the deprivation of bodily pleasures previously lawfully enjoyed.

Of these, some are capital, some less than capital. Capital is the infliction of death, either simply or with torment. Less than capital are stripes, wounds, chains, and any other bodily pain not in its own nature mortal. For if upon the infliction of a punishment death does not follow in the intention of the one inflicting it, the punishment is not to be reckoned capital, even if the harm proves mortal by some accident not to be foreseen; in that case death is not inflicted but hastened.

Financial punishment is that which consists not only in the loss of a sum of money, but also of lands, or any other goods usually bought and sold for money. If the law that ordains such a punishment is made with the design of gathering money from those who shall transgress it, it is not properly a punishment but the price of privilege and exemption from the law — which does not absolutely forbid the act, but only forbids it to those who cannot pay the money. The exception is where the law is natural, or part of religion; for in that case it is not an exemption from the law but a transgression of it. As where a law imposes a financial fine on those who take the name of God in vain, the payment of the fine is not the price of a dispensation to swear, but the punishment of the transgression of a law that cannot be dispensed with. In the same way, if the law imposes a sum of money to be paid to the man who has been injured, this is only a satisfaction for the hurt done him; and it extinguishes the accusation of the injured party, not the crime of the offender.

Ignominy is the infliction of such an evil as is made dishonourable, or the deprivation of such good as is made honourable, by the commonwealth. For there are some things honourable by nature — the effects of courage, magnanimity, strength, wisdom, and other abilities of body and mind; others are made honourable by the commonwealth — badges, titles, offices, or any other singular mark of the sovereign's favour. The first (though they may fail through nature or accident) cannot be taken away by a law; and so the loss of them is not punishment. But the latter may be taken away by the public authority that made them honourable, and are properly punishments. Such are the degrading of condemned men from their badges, titles, and offices, or the declaring of them incapable of the like in time to come.

Imprisonment is when a man is by public authority deprived of liberty; and may happen for two different ends — one being the safe custody of a man accused, the other being the inflicting of pain on a man condemned. The former is not punishment, because no man is supposed to be punished before he has been judicially heard and declared guilty. So whatever hurt a man is made to suffer by bonds or restraint before his case is heard, beyond what is necessary to secure his custody, is against the law of nature. But the latter is punishment, being an evil inflicted by public authority for something that has by the same authority been judged a transgression of the law. Under the word 'imprisonment' I include all restraint of motion caused by an external obstacle — be it a house (which goes by the general name of prison), or an island (when men are said to be confined to it), or a place where men are set to work (as in old times when men were condemned to the quarries, and in our times to the galleys), or be it a chain, or any other such impediment.

Exile, or banishment, is when a man is for a crime condemned to depart out of the dominion of the commonwealth, or out of a certain part of it, and during a fixed time, or for ever, not to return into it. In its own nature, without other circumstances, it does not seem to be a punishment, but rather an escape, or a public command to avoid punishment by flight. Cicero says there was never any such punishment ordained in the city of Rome, but he calls it a refuge of men in danger. For if a man banished is still permitted to enjoy his goods and the revenue of his lands, the mere change of air is no punishment; nor does it tend to the benefit of the commonwealth, for which all punishments are ordained (that is, to forming men's wills to the observance of the law) — but often to the damage of the commonwealth. For a banished man is a lawful enemy of the commonwealth that banished him, since he is no longer a member of it. But if he is also deprived of his lands or goods, then the punishment lies not in the exile, but is to be reckoned among financial punishments.

All punishments of innocent subjects, be they great or small, are against the law of nature. For punishment is only of the transgression of the law, and so there can be no punishment of the innocent. It is therefore a violation, first, of that law of nature which forbids all men in their revenges to look at anything but some future good — for there can come no good to the commonwealth from punishing the innocent. Second, of the law that forbids ingratitude: since all sovereign power is originally given by the consent of every one of the subjects, to the end that they should, so long as they are obedient, be protected by it, the punishment of the innocent is a rendering of evil for good. And third, of the law that commands equity — that is, an equal distribution of justice — which is not observed in punishing the innocent.

But the infliction of any evil whatever on an innocent man who is not a subject, if it is for the benefit of the commonwealth and without violation of any prior covenant, is no breach of the law of nature. For all men who are not subjects are either enemies, or else they have ceased to be enemies by some prior covenant. But against enemies whom the commonwealth judges able to do it hurt, it is lawful, by the original right of nature, to make war; in which the sword does not judge, nor does the victor make distinction of guilty and innocent as to time past, nor has any other regard to mercy than as it conduces to the good of his own people. And on this ground it is that even in subjects who deliberately deny the authority of the established commonwealth, the vengeance is lawfully extended not only to the fathers but also to the third and fourth generation not yet in being, and consequently innocent of the act for which they suffer. Because the nature of this offence consists in the renouncing of subjection, which is a relapse into the condition of war, commonly called rebellion; and those who so offend suffer not as subjects but as enemies. For rebellion is only war renewed.

REWARD is either of gift or by contract. When by contract, it is called salary and wages — a benefit due for service performed or promised. When of gift, it is a benefit proceeding from the grace of those who bestow it, to encourage or enable men to do them service. And so when the sovereign of a commonwealth appoints a salary for any public office, the man who receives it is bound in justice to perform that office; otherwise he is only bound in honour to acknowledge it, and to endeavour to repay it. For though men have no lawful remedy when they are commanded to leave their private business to serve the public without reward or salary, they are not bound to it by the law of nature, nor by the institution of the commonwealth, unless the service cannot otherwise be done — because the sovereign is supposed to be able to make use of all their means, so that the most common soldier may demand the wages of his warfare as a debt.

The benefits which a sovereign bestows on a subject from fear of some power, and ability, the subject has to do harm to the commonwealth, are not properly rewards. They are not salaries, because no contract is supposed in this case, every man being already obliged not to do the commonwealth disservice. Nor are they graces, because they are extorted by fear — which ought not to be incident to the sovereign power. They are rather sacrifices which the sovereign (considered in his natural person, not in the person of the commonwealth) makes for the appeasing of the discontent of one he thinks more powerful than himself; and they encourage not obedience but, on the contrary, the continuance and increase of further extortion.

Whereas some salaries are certain, and proceed from the public treasure, and others uncertain and casual, proceeding from the execution of the office for which the salary is ordained, the latter is in some cases hurtful to the commonwealth — as in the case of judicature. For where the benefit of the judges and ministers of a court of justice arises from the multitude of cases brought to their cognisance, two inconveniences must follow: one, the encouragement of lawsuits, for the more suits, the greater benefit; and another, which depends on that — contention about jurisdiction, each court drawing to itself as many cases as it can. But in offices of execution there are no such inconveniences, because their employment cannot be increased by any effort of their own. And this much shall suffice for the nature of punishment and reward — which are, as it were, the nerves and tendons that move the limbs and joints of a commonwealth.

Up to this point I have set forth the nature of man (whose pride and other passions have compelled him to submit himself to government), together with the great power of his governor, whom I compared to Leviathan, taking that comparison out of the last two verses of the forty-first chapter of Job, where God, having set forth the great power of Leviathan, calls him king of the proud. 'There is nothing,' he says, 'on earth to be compared with him. He is made so as not to be afraid. He sees every high thing below him; and is king of all the children of pride.' But because he is mortal, and subject to decay, as all other earthly creatures are; and because there is something in heaven (though not on earth) that he should stand in fear of, and whose laws he ought to obey, I shall in the following chapters speak of his diseases, and of the causes of his mortality, and of what laws of nature he is bound to obey.

title: Chapter 29. Of Those Things That Weaken, or Tend to the Dissolution of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: Though nothing that mortals make can be immortal, yet if men had the use of reason they pretend to, their commonwealths might be secured, at least, from perishing by internal diseases. For by the nature of their institution they are designed to live as long as mankind, or as the laws of nature, or as justice itself, which gives them life. So when they come to be dissolved, not by external violence but by internal disorder, the fault is not in men as they are the matter, but as they are the makers and orderers of them. For men, when at last they grow weary of irregular jostling and hewing one another, and desire with all their hearts to conform themselves into one firm and lasting edifice, are nevertheless unable — for want both of the art of making fit laws to square their actions by, and of the humility and patience to suffer the rude and cumbersome points of their present greatness to be planed off — to be assembled, without the help of a very able architect, into anything but a crazy building, which can hardly last out their own time and must inevitably fall on the heads of their posterity.

Among the infirmities of a commonwealth, then, I will reckon in the first place those that arise from an imperfect institution, and resemble the diseases of a natural body which proceed from a defective procreation.

Of which this is one: 'That a man to obtain a kingdom is sometimes content with less power than is necessarily required for the peace and defence of the commonwealth.' From this it follows that when the power thus set aside has, for public safety, to be resumed, the resumption has the look of an unjust act — which disposes great numbers of men, when occasion is presented, to rebel; just as the bodies of children begotten by diseased parents are subject either to untimely death or to purging the ill quality derived from their vicious conception by breaking out into boils and scabs. When kings deny themselves some such necessary power, it is not always (though sometimes) out of ignorance of what is necessary to the office they undertake, but often out of a hope to recover the same again at their pleasure. In which they do not reason well; for those who hold them to their promises shall be backed against them by foreign commonwealths, which, for the good of their own subjects, let slip few occasions to weaken the estate of their neighbours. So Thomas Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, was supported against Henry the Second by the pope — the subjection of churchmen to the commonwealth having been dispensed with by William the Conqueror at his accession, when he took an oath not to infringe the liberty of the Church. So too the barons, whose power had been raised by William Rufus (to gain their help in transferring the succession from his elder brother to himself) to a degree inconsistent with the sovereign power, were upheld in their rebellion against King John by the French. Nor does this happen in monarchy alone. For whereas the style of the ancient Roman commonwealth was 'the Senate and people of Rome,' neither the Senate nor the people claimed the whole power; and this first caused the seditions of Tiberius Gracchus, Gaius Gracchus, Lucius Saturninus, and others; and afterwards the wars between the Senate and the people, under Marius and Sulla, and again under Pompey and Caesar, leading to the extinction of their democracy and the setting up of monarchy.

The people of Athens bound themselves from one action only — that no man, on pain of death, should propose the renewing of the war for the island of Salamis; and yet even by that, if Solon had not caused it to be given out that he was mad, and afterwards, in the gesture and dress of a madman, proposed it in verse to the people who flocked around him, they would have had an enemy perpetually in readiness at the very gates of their city. Such are the damages, or evasions, that all commonwealths are reduced to whose power is even slightly limited.

In the second place, I take notice of the diseases of a commonwealth that proceed from the poison of seditious doctrines, of which one is: 'That every private man is judge of good and evil actions.' This is true in the condition of mere nature, where there are no civil laws; and also under civil government, in such cases as are not determined by the law. But otherwise, it is plain that the measure of good and evil actions is the civil law, and the judge is the legislator, who is always the representative of the commonwealth. From this false doctrine, men are disposed to debate with themselves, and to dispute the commands of the commonwealth, and afterwards to obey or disobey them as in their private judgement they shall think fit; by which the commonwealth is distracted and weakened.

Another doctrine repugnant to civil society is that 'whatever a man does against his conscience is sin' — and it depends on the presumption of making oneself judge of good and evil. For a man's conscience and his judgement are the same thing; and as the judgement, so also the conscience may be erroneous. So though the man who is subject to no civil law sins in all he does against his conscience (because he has no other rule to follow but his own reason), it is not so for the man who lives in a commonwealth, because the law is the public conscience, by which he has already undertaken to be guided. Otherwise, given the diversity that there is of private consciences, which are only private opinions, the commonwealth must inevitably be distracted, and no man would dare to obey the sovereign power any further than it shall seem good in his own eyes.

It has also been commonly taught 'that faith and sanctity are not to be attained by study and reason, but by supernatural inspiration, or infusion.' Granted that, I do not see why any man should give a reason for his faith, or why every Christian should not also be a prophet, or why any man should take the law of his country, rather than his own inspiration, as the rule of his action. And so we fall again into the fault of taking upon ourselves to judge of good and evil, or of making such private men as claim to be supernaturally inspired into judges of it — to the dissolution of all civil government. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by those accidents that bring us into the presence of those who speak to us; and these accidents are all contrived by God Almighty, and yet are not supernatural, but only — because of the great number of them concurring in every effect — unobservable. Faith and sanctity are indeed not very frequent, but they are not miracles; they are brought about by education, discipline, correction, and other natural ways, by which God works them in his elect at such time as he thinks fit. And these three opinions, harmful to peace and to government, have in this part of the world proceeded chiefly from the tongues and pens of unlearned divines, who, joining the words of Holy Scripture together other than as agrees with reason, do what they can to make men think that sanctity and natural reason cannot stand together.

A fourth opinion, repugnant to the nature of a commonwealth, is this: 'That the holder of the sovereign power is subject to the civil laws.' It is true that sovereigns are all subject to the laws of nature, because those laws are divine and cannot be abrogated by any man or commonwealth. But to those laws which the sovereign himself — that is, which the commonwealth — makes, he is not subject. For to be subject to the laws is to be subject to the commonwealth, that is, to the sovereign representative — that is, to himself; which is not subjection but freedom from the laws. This error, because it sets the laws above the sovereign, also sets a judge above him, and a power to punish him — which is to make a new sovereign; and again, for the same reason, a third, to punish the second; and so on without end, to the confusion and dissolution of the commonwealth.

A fifth doctrine that tends to the dissolution of a commonwealth is that 'every private man has an absolute property in his goods, such as excludes the right of the sovereign.' Every man indeed has a property that excludes the right of every other subject; and he has it only from the sovereign power, without whose protection every other man would have an equal right to the same. But if the right of the sovereign is also excluded, he cannot perform the office they have put him into — which is to defend them both from foreign enemies and from the injuries of one another — and consequently there is no longer a commonwealth.

And if the property of subjects does not exclude the right of the sovereign representative to their goods, much less to their offices of judicature or execution, in which they represent the sovereign himself.

There is a sixth doctrine, plainly and directly against the essence of a commonwealth, and it is this: 'That the sovereign power may be divided.' For what is it to divide the power of a commonwealth, but to dissolve it? — for powers divided mutually destroy each other. And for these doctrines, men are chiefly beholden to some of those who, professing the laws, endeavour to make them depend on their own learning, and not on the legislative power.

And as false doctrine, so also often the example of a different form of government in a neighbouring nation disposes men to alter the form already settled. So the people of the Jews were stirred up to reject God, and to call on the prophet Samuel for a king after the manner of the nations. So also the lesser cities of Greece were continually disturbed with seditions of the aristocratic and democratic factions; one part of almost every commonwealth desiring to imitate the Lacedaemonians, the other the Athenians. And I do not doubt that many men were content to see the late troubles in England out of an imitation of the Low Countries, supposing that to grow rich no more was needed than to change, as they had done, the form of government. For the constitution of human nature is of itself subject to a desire for novelty; and when men are prodded toward that by the neighbourhood of those who have been enriched by it, it is almost impossible for them not to be content with those who urge them to change, and to love the first beginnings, even though they are aggrieved by the continuance of the disorder — like hot-blooded men who, having got the itch, tear themselves with their own nails until they can endure the smart no longer.

And as for rebellion in particular against monarchy: one of its most frequent causes is the reading of the books of politics and histories of the ancient Greeks and Romans; from which young men, and all others unprovided with the antidote of solid reason, receiving a strong and delightful impression of the great exploits of war achieved by the leaders of their armies, also receive a pleasing idea of all those leaders did besides — and imagine that their great prosperity proceeded, not from the rivalry of particular men, but from the virtue of their popular form of government; not considering the frequent seditions and civil wars produced by the imperfection of their politics. From the reading, I say, of such books, men have undertaken to kill their kings, because the Greek and Latin writers in their books and discussions of politics make it lawful, and laudable, for any man to do so, provided that before doing it he calls the king a tyrant. For they do not say regicide — that is, the killing of a king — but tyrannicide, the killing of a tyrant, is lawful. From the same books, those who live under a monarch take up the opinion that the subjects in a popular commonwealth enjoy liberty, but that in a monarchy they are all slaves. I say it is those who live under a monarchy who take up such an opinion, not those who live under a popular government — for they find no such thing. In short, I cannot imagine how anything can be more prejudicial to a monarchy than allowing such books to be publicly read without immediately applying such correctives as discreet teachers can fit to take away their venom; a venom I will not hesitate to compare to the bite of a mad dog — a disease the physicians call hydrophobia, or fear of water. For as the man so bitten has a continual torment of thirst, and yet abhors water, and is in such a state as if the poison were trying to turn him into a dog, so when a monarchy has once been bitten to the quick by those democratical writers who continually snarl at that estate, it wants nothing more than a strong monarch — yet, when it has him, out of a certain tyrannophobia, a fear of being strongly governed, it abhors him.

As there have been doctors who hold that there are three souls in a man, so also there are those who think that there may be more souls (that is, more sovereigns) than one in a commonwealth; and they set up a supremacy against the sovereignty, canons against laws, and a ghostly authority against the civil, working on men's minds with words and distinctions that in themselves signify nothing, but betray (by their obscurity) that there walks (as some think invisibly) another kingdom — a kind of kingdom of fairies in the dark. Now since it is plain that the civil power and the power of the commonwealth are the same thing, and that supremacy, and the power of making canons and granting faculties, implies a commonwealth, it follows that where one is sovereign and another supreme, where one can make laws and another make canons, there must be two commonwealths over one and the same subjects, which is a kingdom divided in itself and cannot stand. For notwithstanding the insignificant distinction between 'temporal' and 'ghostly,' they are still two kingdoms, and every subject is subject to two masters. For seeing the ghostly power claims the right to declare what is sin, it claims by consequence the right to declare what is law (sin being nothing but the transgression of the law); and again, the civil power claiming to declare what is law, every subject must obey two masters, who will both have their commands observed as law — which is impossible. Or, if it is only one kingdom, either the civil (which is the power of the commonwealth) must be subordinate to the ghostly, or the ghostly subordinate to the temporal — and then there is no supremacy but the temporal. So when these two powers oppose one another, the commonwealth cannot but be in great danger of civil war and dissolution. For the civil authority, being more visible and standing in the clearer light of natural reason, cannot but draw to it at all times a very considerable part of the people; and the spiritual, though it stands in the darkness of school distinctions and hard words, yet, because the fear of darkness and ghosts is greater than other fears, cannot lack a party sufficient to trouble, and sometimes to destroy, a commonwealth. And this is a disease which not unfitly may be compared to the epilepsy, or falling-sickness (which the Jews took to be one kind of possession by spirits), in the natural body. For as in this disease there is an unnatural spirit, or wind, in the head, which obstructs the roots of the nerves and, moving them violently, takes away the motion they should naturally have from the power of the soul in the brain, and so causes violent and irregular motions (which men call convulsions) in the parts, so that a man seized with it falls down sometimes into the water and sometimes into the fire, as one deprived of his senses; so also in the body politic, when the spiritual power moves the members of a commonwealth by the terror of punishments and the hope of rewards (which are its nerves) otherwise than by the civil power (which is the soul of the commonwealth) they ought to be moved, and by strange and hard words suffocates the people, it either overwhelms the commonwealth with oppression, or casts it into the fire of a civil war.

Sometimes also in the merely civil government there is more than one soul: as when the power of levying money (which is the nutritive faculty) has depended on a general assembly; the power of conduct and command (which is the motive faculty) on one man; and the power of making laws (which is the rational faculty) on the accidental consent not only of those two but also of a third. This endangers the commonwealth, sometimes for want of consent to good laws, but most often for want of such nourishment as is necessary to life and motion. For though few perceive that such a government is not government, but a dividing of the commonwealth into three factions, and call it 'mixed monarchy,' the truth is that it is not one independent commonwealth but three independent factions; not one representative person but three. In the kingdom of God there may be three persons independent without breach of unity in God who reigns; but where men reign, who are subject to diversity of opinions, it cannot be so. And so if the king bears the person of the people, and the general assembly bears also the person of the people, and another assembly bears the person of a part of the people, they are not one person, nor one sovereign, but three persons and three sovereigns.

To what disease in the natural body of man I might exactly compare this irregularity of a commonwealth, I do not know. But I have seen a man who had another man growing out of his side, with a head, arms, breast, and stomach of his own: if he had had another man growing out of his other side too, the comparison might then have been exact.

So far I have named such diseases of a commonwealth as are of the greatest and most present danger. There are others, not so great, which are nevertheless not unfit to be noted. First, the difficulty of raising money for the necessary uses of the commonwealth, especially in the approach of war. This difficulty arises from the opinion every subject has of a property in his lands and goods exclusive of the sovereign's right to the use of the same. From this it follows that the sovereign power, which foresees the necessities and dangers of the commonwealth, finding the passage of money to the public treasure obstructed by the tenacity of the people — whereas it ought to extend itself, to meet and prevent such dangers in their beginnings — contracts itself as long as it can, and when it can no longer, struggles with the people by stratagems of law to obtain little sums; and when those will not suffice, is forced at last violently to open the way for present supply, or to perish. And being often put to these extremities, it at last reduces the people to their due temper — or else the commonwealth must perish. So we may compare this distemper very aptly to an ague, in which the fleshy parts, being congealed or by venomous matter obstructed, leave the veins which by their natural course empty themselves into the heart unsupplied (as they ought to be) from the arteries; whereby there first comes a cold contraction and trembling of the limbs, and afterwards a hot and strong endeavour of the heart to force a passage for the blood; and before it can do that, it contents itself with the small refreshment of such things as cool for a time, till (if nature is strong enough) it at last breaks the contumacy of the parts obstructed, and disperses the venom in sweat; or (if nature is too weak) the patient dies.

Again, there is sometimes in a commonwealth a disease which resembles pleurisy: namely, when the treasure of the commonwealth, flowing out of its due course, is gathered together in too much abundance in one, or a few, private men, by monopolies or by the farming of the public revenues — just as the blood in pleurisy, getting into the membrane of the breast, breeds there an inflammation, accompanied with a fever and painful stitches.

Also, the popularity of a powerful subject (unless the commonwealth has very good security of his fidelity) is a dangerous disease; because the people, who should receive their motion from the authority of the sovereign, are drawn away by the flattery and the reputation of an ambitious man from their obedience to the laws, to follow a man whose virtues and designs they have no knowledge of. And this is commonly more dangerous in a popular government than in a monarchy, since they can easily be made to believe that they are the people. By this means it was that Julius Caesar, who was set up by the people against the Senate, having won to himself the affections of his army, made himself master of both the Senate and the people. And this proceeding of popular and ambitious men is plain rebellion, and may be likened to the effects of witchcraft.

Another infirmity of a commonwealth is the immoderate greatness of a town, when it is able to furnish out of its own precincts the number and expense of a great army; as also the great number of corporations, which are, as it were, many lesser commonwealths in the bowels of a greater, like worms in the entrails of a natural man.

To which may be added the liberty of disputing against absolute power, by pretenders to political prudence — who, though for the most part bred in the dregs of the people, yet, animated by false doctrines, are perpetually meddling with the fundamental laws, to the vexation of the commonwealth, like the little worms which physicians call ascarides.

We may further add the insatiable appetite, or bulimia, of enlarging dominion, with the incurable wounds often received from the enemy in pursuit of it; and the wens of unannexed conquests, which are many times a burden, and with less danger lost than kept; and likewise the lethargy of ease, and the consumption of riotous and vain expense.

Lastly, when in a war (foreign or internal) the enemies have won a final victory — so that the forces of the commonwealth, keeping the field no longer, can no longer protect their subjects in their loyalty — then is the commonwealth DISSOLVED, and every man at liberty to protect himself by such courses as his own discretion shall suggest. For the sovereign is the public soul, giving life and motion to the commonwealth; which once expiring, the members are no more governed by it than the carcase of a man is governed by his departed (though immortal) soul. For though the right of a sovereign monarch cannot be extinguished by the act of another, the obligation of the members may be. For he who wants protection may seek it anywhere; and when he has it, he is obliged (without any fraudulent pretence of having submitted himself out of fear) to protect his protection as long as he is able. But when the power of an assembly is once suppressed, the right of the same perishes utterly, because the assembly itself is extinct; and consequently there is no possibility for the sovereignty to re-enter.
